key_insight: The paper argues that long-horizon autoregressive video generation fails when models cannot remember important past events under limited context and compute. It proposes treating memory as a core design element so generated videos can stay consistent over time.
problem_solved: Autoregressive video models must generate extended sequences with fixed context windows and limited storage/computation, which causes them to forget crucial historical details like object identities, scene state, and temporal continuity.
method: Analyze memory limitations in autoregressive video rollout under bounded context and resource constraints.
Introduce a memory-aware generation framework to preserve key historical information across long sequences.
Use stored past frames or summaries to improve consistency, identity preservation, and long-term temporal coherence.
impact: This matters for practitioners building long-video generators, interactive simulators, and world models because it helps reduce drift and inconsistency over time. Better memory handling can make generated videos more realistic, stable, and usable for downstream applications.
visual_elements: A timeline showing how information is lost across long autoregressive rollouts
A comparison diagram of short context vs. memory-augmented generation
An icon-based flowchart of frame generation, memory storage, and retrieval
Before/after visual examples highlighting identity and scene consistency
paper_title: The Past Frames the Future: Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation
paper_authors: Harold Haodong Chen, Rongjin Guo, Disen Lan, Wen-Jie Shu, Hongfei Zhang
